## Appendix A On the regularity conditions for Proposition 3.3

Here we provide a more detailed justification that our regularity assumptions for Proposition 3.3 are sufficient. Specifically, the proof of Proposition 3.3 requires

- (i) the Fisher information of $\mu$ to be well-defined and finite, and

- (ii) for a Cramér-Rao type lower bound to hold for each $\pi_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ given by $d\pi_{x}^{\varepsilon}(y)=k_{\mu}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)d\mu(y)$ .

If $\mu$ has a density $\rho$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure and $\sqrt{\rho}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , then its Fisher information

$$ I(\mu)\vcentcolon=4\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\|\nabla\sqrt{\rho}\right\|^{2}dx $$

is finite. In particular, $\sqrt{\rho}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ requires $\sqrt{\rho}$ to be weakly differentiable, i.e., for an integration by parts identity to hold. The proof of Cramér-Rao also relies heavily on integration by parts. On a bounded domain, integration by parts is Green’s identity, which typically involves a boundary integral unless appropriate boundary conditions are imposed. We argue that both (i) and (ii) hold under the assumptions on $\mu$ in Proposition 3.3, which we repeat here for convenience.

#### Assumption A.1.

Suppose $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is a bounded open set with $C^{1}$ boundary, and $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\overline{\Omega})$ has density $\rho$ (with respect to the Lebesgue measure) satisfying:

- – $\rho(x)>0$ for $x\in\Omega$ ,

- – $\rho(x)=0$ for $x\in\partial\Omega$ ,

- – $\widetilde{\rho}\vcentcolon=\sqrt{\rho}\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})$ .

We also define $W(x)\vcentcolon=-\log\rho(x)=-2\log\widetilde{\rho}(x)$ for $x\in\Omega$ , i.e., $\rho(x)=e^{-W(x)}$ on $\Omega$ .

Due to the boundary condition $\widetilde{\rho}(x)=0$ for $x\in\partial\Omega$ , we have, for any $\varphi\in C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})$ ,

$$ \int_{\Omega}\varphi(x)\nabla\widetilde{\rho}(x)dx=-\int_{\Omega}\widetilde{\rho}(x)\nabla\varphi(x)dx $$

by Green’s identity (e.g., [13, Appendix C.2]). Therefore $\widetilde{\rho}=\sqrt{\rho}$ (extended naturally to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ by $\widetilde{\rho}(x)=0$ for $x\notin\overline{\Omega}$ ) is weakly differentiable and, as $\Omega$ is bounded, $\widetilde{\rho}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . In fact, this only required $\widetilde{\rho}\in C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})$ .

We now show that a Cramér-Rao lower bound for $\mu$ holds under Assumption A.1.

#### Lemma A.1.

Under Assumption A.1, $\nabla^{2}W$ is integrable with respect to $\mu$ , $\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\nabla^{2}W\right]$ is positive definite, and

$$ \mathrm{Cov}_{X\sim\mu}(X)\succeq\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\nabla^{2}W\right]\right)^{-1}. $$

#### Remark A.1.

Recall that we would like to apply Cramér-Rao to $d\pi_{x}^{\varepsilon}=k_{\mu}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)d\mu(y)$ . If $\mu$ satisfies Assumption A.1, then $\pi_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ has density

$$ y\mapsto k_{\mu}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\rho(y)=\exp\left(\frac{f_{\mu,\mu}^{\varepsilon}(x)+f_{\mu,\mu}^{\varepsilon}(y)-\|x-y\|^{2}}{\varepsilon}\right)\rho(y). $$

Since $f_{\mu,\mu}^{\varepsilon}$ is smooth (recall the representation (9)), each $\pi_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ satisfies Assumption A.1 whenever $\mu$ does, so we can apply Lemma A.1 to $\pi_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ .

The proof is similar to [10]. However, as we are working with a bounded domain $\Omega$ and $W$ goes to infinity as one approaches the boundary $\partial\Omega$ , we provide additional details to justify the Cramér-Rao inequality under Assumption A.1.

#### Proof of Lemma A.1.

First we check that $\nabla^{2}W$ is integrable with respect to $\mu$ . For this, it is convenient to write the derivatives of $W=-2\log\widetilde{\rho}$ in terms of $\widetilde{\rho}$ :

$$ \frac{\partial W}{\partial x_{k}}=-\frac{2}{\widetilde{\rho}}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{k}} $$

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}W}{\partial x_{k}\partial x_{l}}=-2\left(-\frac{1}{\widetilde{\rho}^{2}}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{l}}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{k}}+\frac{1}{\widetilde{\rho}}\frac{\partial^{2}\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{k}\partial x_{l}}\right) $$

on $\Omega$ . As $\widetilde{\rho}^{2}=\rho$ and $\widetilde{\rho}\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})$ , we have that each $\frac{\partial^{2}W}{\partial x_{k}\partial x_{l}}$ is integrable with respect to $\mu$ and

$$ \int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial^{2}W}{\partial x_{k}\partial x_{l}}\rho(x)dx=2\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{l}}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{k}}-\widetilde{\rho}\frac{\partial^{2}\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{k}\partial x_{l}}dx=4\int_{\Omega}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{l}}\frac{\partial\widetilde{\rho}}{\partial x_{k}}dx, $$

where the last equality holds by Green’s identity with the boundary condition $\widetilde{\rho}(x)=0$ for $x\in\partial\Omega$ . Modifying the proof from [10], let us fix any non-zero vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and take $h\vcentcolon=\langle w,\cdot\rangle$ . Then

$$ w=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla h]=\int_{\Omega}\rho(x)\nabla h(x)dx=-\int_{\Omega}h(x)\nabla\rho(x)dx $$

$$ \int_{\Omega}\nabla\rho(x)dx=0 $$

again by Green’s identity and the boundary condition $\rho(x)=0$ for $x\in\partial\Omega$ . Therefore

$$ w=-\int_{\Omega}(h(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])\nabla\rho(x)dx=-2\int_{\Omega}(h(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])\widetilde{\rho}(x)\nabla\widetilde{\rho}(x)dx, $$

so that

$$ \|w\|^{2}=-2\int_{\Omega}(h(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])\widetilde{\rho}(x)w^{\top}\nabla\widetilde{\rho}(x)dx. $$

Applying Cauchy-Schwarz to the right-hand side gives us

$$ \displaystyle\|w\|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left(\int_{\Omega}(h(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])^{2}\widetilde{\rho}^{2}(x)dx\right)^{1/2}\left(4\int_{\Omega}(w^{\top}\nabla\widetilde{\rho}(x))^{2}dx\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle=\left(\mathrm{Var}_{\mu}(h)\right)^{1/2}\left(w^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]w\right)^{1/2} $$

since $\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]$ is given by (62). As $\mathrm{Var}_{\mu}(h)=\int_{\Omega}(h(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])^{2}\rho(x)dx>0$ , we have that $\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]$ is strictly positive definite, so that

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle w,\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]^{-1}w\right\rangle \displaystyle=-2\int_{\Omega}(h(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])\widetilde{\rho}(x)\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]^{-1}w\right)^{\top}\nabla\widetilde{\rho}(x)dx \displaystyle\leq\left(\mathrm{Var}_{\mu}(h)\right)^{1/2}\left(4\int_{\Omega}\left(\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]^{-1}w\right)^{\top}\nabla\widetilde{\rho}(x)\right)^{2}dx\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle=\left(\mathrm{Var}_{\mu}(h)\right)^{1/2}\left(\left\langle w,\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nabla^{2}W]^{-1}w\right\rangle\right)^{1/2} $$

by another application of Cauchy-Schwarz. (61) follows from rearranging. ∎
